# PROP 2: Increases State’s Rainy Day Fund

[Download PDF](<https://hoover-s3-website.s3.us-west-2.amazonaws.com/s3fs-public/2026-10/California Decides_Proposition 2.pdf>) 

[Research](#researchareas) 

*   [Quick Facts](#facts)
*   [Key Questions](#key-questions)
*   [Risks & Benefits](#risks)

[California Decides](https://cms.hoover.org/publications/california-decides) 

###### Quick Facts

*   **Official ballot title:** “Increases State’s Rainy Day Fund.” (Assembly Constitutional Amendment 20, Resolution Chapter 130, Statutes of 2026). The measure’s own name is the “Save for California’s Future Act.”
*   **Type:** Legislatively referred constitutional amendment (a two-thirds vote of each house placed it on the ballot). It will pass with a simple majority.
*   **A vote YES means:** California would double the maximum size of its rainy-day fund from 10 percent to 20 percent of general fund tax revenues. It would also capture more money in years when capital-gains revenue spikes, extend mandatory extra debt payments through the 2039–40 fiscal year, and count rainy-day deposits against the Gann limit on state spending in the year the money is withdrawn and spent.
*   **A vote NO means:** The current rainy-day fund rules stay in place. The reserve remains capped at 10 percent of general fund tax revenues, and the requirement to split certain deposits between savings and extra debt payments expires after the 2029–30 fiscal year.
*   **Sponsor/proponent:** Legislative Democrats and Governor Gavin Newsome. Lead authors are Assemblymembers Jesse Gabriel and Avelino Valencia and Senators Melissa Hurtado and John Laird, with support from Assembly Speaker Robert Rivas and the governor’s administration.
*   **On the ballot because:** The Legislature passed ACA 20 by the required two-thirds margin on June 25, 2026. The Senate vote was twenty-nine to two and the Assembly fifty-nine to eight.
*   **Full legal text:** [Assembly Constitutional Amendment 20 (2025–2026), California Legislative Information](https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billTextClient.xhtml?bill_id=202520260ACA20)
*   **LAO analysis:** [Proposition 2 (2026), Legislative Analyst’s Office](https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Proposition?number=2&year=2026)

###### 1\. What would it do?

Proposition 2 would enlarge California’s constitutional savings account, the Budget Stabilization Account, better known as the rainy-day fund. That fund already exists. Voters created its current form in 2014, and it is fed by automatic deposits each year. Proposition 2 does not create a new fund. It changes rules that govern how big the fund can grow, how fast it fills during good years, and how long the state keeps paying down old debts alongside it. Notably it also changes how deposits are treated under the Gann limit on state spending.

The headline change is the deposit cap. Today the state must keep making deposits until the rainy-day fund reaches 10 percent of general fund tax revenues. Once it hits that ceiling, extra money that would have gone into savings is instead spent on infrastructure. Proposition 2 raises the ceiling to 20 percent, so the state can keep saving until the fund is roughly twice as large as it can be under current law.

The second change targets boom years. California leans heavily on personal income taxes tied to capital gains, which rise and fall with the stock market. Current law captures capital-gains revenue above 8 percent of general fund tax revenues and steers it into savings and debt paydown. Proposition 2 keeps that trigger and adds a steeper tier on top of it. For the slice of capital-gains revenue above 10 percent of general fund tax revenues, the state would set aside 150 percent of that amount, pulling even more out of the biggest windfalls.

The third change is timing. Under a rule that began in 2015, half of these deposits go into the reserve and the other half pays down long-term debts such as pension and retiree-health obligations. That split is set to expire after the 2029–30 fiscal year. Proposition 2 extends it through the 2039–40 fiscal year. The eligible debts would include current and future school-funding settle-up payments owed under Proposition 98, money the general fund borrows from the state’s own special funds, and the state’s federal unemployment insurance loan, which stands at roughly $20 billion. The last two changes are new. Starting in 2027–28, deposits into the rainy-day fund would count against the state appropriations limit, known as the Gann limit, only when the money is withdrawn. Today they count when deposited.

 

###### 2\. The legal language

*   **Full text:** [Assembly Constitutional Amendment 20, “Save for California’s Future Act,” Resolution Chapter 130, Statutes of 2026, California Legislative Information](https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billTextClient.xhtml?bill_id=202520260ACA20)
*   **Key language:**

“\[T\]he amount of a transfer to the Budget Stabilization Account … for any fiscal year shall not exceed an amount that would result in a balance in the account that, when the transfer is made, exceeds 20 percent of the amount of General Fund proceeds of taxes for the fiscal year.” The paragraphs cited are the required transfers, so voluntary deposits fall outside the cap.

On the steeper capture of capital-gains spikes, the amendment directs the state to set aside the sum of “the portion of the estimate … that is in excess of 8 percent, but not in excess of 10 percent” plus “150 percent of the portion of the estimate … in excess of 10 percent” of general fund proceeds of taxes.

On the Gann limit, the amendment provides that starting in the 2027–28 fiscal year, “transfers to the Budget Stabilization Account shall not constitute ‘appropriations subject to limitation’ for purposes of Article XIII B.” Money withdrawn later counts “in the fiscal year in which \[it is\] withdrawn.”

*   **What it amends:** Amends Sections 20 and 22 of Article XVI of the California Constitution, the article that governs state finance and the rainy-day fund. Because it is a constitutional amendment, the legislature cannot repeal or alter it without returning to the voters.

 

###### 3\. What, Where, When, Why?

*   **Who?** Authored by Assemblymembers Jesse Gabriel and Avelino Valencia and Senators Melissa Hurtado and John Laird, all Democrats, and championed by Assembly Speaker Robert Rivas with backing from the governor’s administration. It passed the legislature on largely party lines, with only two recorded Senate no votes.

*   **What?** Raises the rainy-day deposit cap from 10 percent to 20 percent of general fund tax revenues, captures 150 percent of the largest capital-gains spikes, extends the required extra debt payments from 2029–30 through 2039–40, and counts rainy-day deposits against the Gann limit only when the money is withdrawn.
*   **Where?** Statewide, written into Article XVI of the California Constitution.
*   **When?** On the November 3, 2026, ballot. If passed, the new deposit and Gann limit rules would apply starting in the 2027–28 fiscal year and the extended debt-paydown split would run through 2039–40.
*   **Why?** Proponents point to California’s volatile, top-heavy revenue base and the recurring deficits that follow every downturn. Their stated goal is to save more in good years so the state can protect schools, healthcare, and public safety without deep cuts or new taxes when revenues fall. The argument against calls the larger fund a “slush fund” and argues that moving deposits outside the Gann limit makes the taxpayer rebates it requires less likely.

###### 4\. Trade-offs

California’s revenue system is genuinely volatile, and that volatility is not a matter of opinion. The state relies heavily on personal income taxes from its highest earners, whose incomes rise and fall sharply with capital gains and the stock market. That design produces windfalls in boom years and sudden shortfalls in downturns. Reserves built under the 2014 rainy-day fund measurably softened the blow in the 2020 pandemic recession, and they were drawn down again as the state faced multibillion-dollar deficits in the years since, including an estimated $18 billion gap heading into 2026–27. A bigger fund that fills faster in boom years is a direct answer to a real and repeated problem.

But saving is not free. Every dollar the constitution steers into the reserve or toward extra debt payments is a dollar not available this year for schools, healthcare, child care, or tax relief. Raising the ceiling from 10 to 20 percent and capturing 150 percent of the biggest capital-gains spikes means more revenue is locked away by formula rather than appropriated through the annual budget.

Opponents object because of its effects on the Gann limit. Under the Gann limit, adopted by voters in 1979, revenue above the limit over two years must be split between taxpayer rebates and schools. Rainy-day deposits count as spending under the Gann limit today. Proposition 2 would stop counting them until they are withdrawn, which gives the state more room under the Gann limit in boom years and makes rebates less likely. The state had $27 billion of room under the Gann limit in 2026–27, so the change matters most in years when revenue surges past it.

Two further points deserve consideration. First, a larger cap does not guarantee the money will be there when a recession hits, because the constitution still lets the governor declare a budget emergency and the legislature can suspend or draw down deposits. A bigger fund raises the ceiling on saving, but it does not force the state to keep the money saved. Second, the most concrete and least disputed piece of the measure is the debt-paydown extension. Pension liabilities, retiree health obligations, and federal unemployment-insurance loans are real debts that accrue interest, and paying them down earlier has a measurable, defensible payoff regardless of where one lands on the reserve question. The reserve expansion is the contested part. The debt paydown is the part most budget analysts across the spectrum tend to endorse.

## 5\. Potential risks and benefits

**Potential benefits**

*   A larger reserve gives the state a bigger cushion against California’s well-documented revenue swings, reducing the depth of cuts or the pressure for new taxes in a downturn.
*   Setting aside 150 percent of the largest capital-gains spikes targets the volatile money that has historically tempted the state into spending commitments it cannot sustain.
*   Counting deposits against the Gann limit only when they are withdrawn removes a penalty on saving. Under current rules, a deposit uses up room under the Gann limit the same way spending does.
*   The Legislative Analyst concludes reserves would be higher and that balancing the budget would be “somewhat easier when revenues decline.”

**Potential risks**

*   Money constitutionally directed into savings and debt is money not available now for schools, healthcare, and other services, a real opportunity cost in years when the budget is tight.
*   A higher cap does not lock the money in place. A governor-declared budget emergency still lets the legislature suspend deposits or draw the fund down, so the reserve may not be there when it is needed.
*   Formula-driven set-asides reduce the legislature’s year-to-year budget flexibility, shifting more spending decisions from elected officials to a constitutional formula.
*   Excluding deposits from the Gann limit makes its taxpayer rebates less likely in boom years. Withdrawals count when spent, but a surge can sit in reserves past the two-year window that triggers rebates.
*   The measure does not address the underlying structural imbalance between ongoing commitments and volatile revenues, so it manages the symptoms of volatility rather than the cause.

## 6\. Open questions

*   How much larger would the reserve actually grow, and how many years of boom revenue would it take to approach the new 20 percent deposit cap?
*   In an average recession, would a doubled cap meaningfully change how deep the state's cuts have to be, or would the emergency-suspension rules blunt the benefit?
*   What current programs or tax choices would be crowded out in the near term by steering more revenue into savings and debt paydown?
*   How much of the extended debt payment would go to new paydown, and how much to settle-up payments and internal loans the state already owes?
*   In a year when revenue surges past the Gann limit, how much would the state move into the rainy-day fund and holding account, and how much smaller would taxpayer rebates be as a result?
*   How would the higher reserve interact with the Proposition 98 school-funding guarantee and the state’s constitutional spending limit in high-revenue years?

###### 7\. The questions to ask before you vote

California saves money in good years so it does not have to gut services in bad ones. Proposition 2 would roughly double how much the state can save and pull more from the biggest windfalls. Before you vote, ask whether a bigger locked-away reserve is worth the dollars it takes off the table for schools, healthcare, and other needs today.

A rainy-day fund only helps if the money is still there when the rain comes. This measure raises the ceiling on saving, but the state can still declare an emergency and spend down the fund. Does Proposition 2 build lasting discipline, or does it mostly raise a limit the legislature can waive when it wants to?

## Bill Start

  

 **Assembly Constitutional Amendment No. 20**

 CHAPTER 130

  

 A resolution to propose to the people of the State of California an amendment to the Constitution of the State, by amending Sections 20 and 22 of Article XVI thereof, relating to state finance. 

  

\[ Filed with Secretary of State  June 25, 2026. \] 

  

## LEGISLATIVE COUNSEL'S DIGEST

  

ACA 20, Gabriel. Save for California’s Future Act.

(1) The California Constitution establishes the Budget Stabilization Account and requires the Controller to transfer from the General Fund to the account, no later than October 1 of each fiscal year, a sum equal to 1.5% of the estimated amount of General Fund revenues for that fiscal year. The Department of Finance is required to report specified information to the Legislature, including (A) an estimate of the amount of General Fund proceeds of taxes that may be appropriated for that fiscal year, (B) an estimate of the portion of that amount that is derived from personal income taxes paid on net capital gains, and (C) the portion of the estimate in (B) that exceeds 8% of the estimate made in (A). Notwithstanding the requirement for the Controller to transfer 1.5% of General Fund revenues for each fiscal year to the account, for the 2015–16 fiscal year to the 2029–30 fiscal year, inclusive, the California Constitution instead requires 50% of that amount and 50% of the amount described in (C) to be transferred to the Budget Stabilization Account. The California Constitution requires the remaining 50% to be appropriated for unfunded liabilities and other specified purposes.

Commencing with the 2027–28 fiscal year, this measure would require the Department of Finance to report the sum of the portion of the estimate in (B) that exceeds 8%, but does not exceed 10%, of the estimate in (A) and 150% of the estimate in (B) that exceeds 10% of the estimate in (A). The measure would require 50% of that sum and 50% of the amount equal to 1.5% of the estimated amount of General Fund revenues for the fiscal year to be transferred to the Budget Stabilization Account each fiscal year until the 2039–40 fiscal year, and it would require the remaining 50% to be appropriated for unfunded liabilities and other specified purposes. The measure would add repayment of federal loans relating to unemployment insurance to the purposes for which the remaining 50% may be appropriated.

The California Constitution limits the amount that is required to be transferred to the Budget Stabilization Account for any fiscal year from exceeding an amount that would result in a balance in the account that, when the transfer is made, exceeds 10% of the estimated amount of the General Fund proceeds of taxes for the fiscal year, as specified.

This measure would increase that limit to 20% of the estimated amount of the General Fund proceeds of taxes for the fiscal year.

(2) The California Constitution creates the Public School System Stabilization Account in the General Fund and requires the Controller to transfer specified amounts from the General Fund to the account. Upon a proclamation by the Governor declaring a budget emergency, the Legislature may suspend or reduce transfers to the Budget Stabilization Account or Public School System Stabilization Account, return funds in the Budget Stabilization Account to the General Fund, and appropriate funds in the Public School System Stabilization Account for the support of school districts and community college districts. The California Constitution defines “budget emergency” for these purposes to mean (A) the existence of conditions of disaster or extreme peril, as declared by the Governor, or (B) a determination by the Governor that estimated resources are inadequate to fund General Fund expenditures for the current or ensuing fiscal year at a level equal to the highest amount of total General Fund expenditures estimated at the time of enactment of any of the three most recent Budget Acts.

The California Constitution requires the Governor, within the first 10 days of each calendar year, to submit to the Legislature a proposed budget for the fiscal year commencing on July 1 of that calendar year. Under existing statutory law, the Director of Finance is required to submit a revised budget proposal to the Legislature on or before May 14.

Under this measure, the revised budget proposal submitted on or before May 14, or any other budgetary revision required to be submitted to the Legislature, would constitute the Governor’s proclamation of a budget emergency if the above-described conditions for a budget emergency exist, and if the budgetary revision proposes to suspend or reduce transfers from the General Fund to the Budget Stabilization Account or Public School System Stabilization Account, return funds in the Budget Stabilization Account to the General Fund, or appropriate money from the Public School System Stabilization Account.

(3) The California Constitution prohibits the total annual appropriations subject to limitation of the State and of each local government from exceeding the appropriations limit of the entity of government for the prior year, adjusted for the change in the cost of living and the change in population. The California Constitution defines “appropriations subject to limitation” of the State for these purposes.

This measure would exclude both of the following from the appropriations subject to limitation of the State commencing with the 2027–28 fiscal year: (A) transfers to the Budget Stabilization Account; and (B) transfers to a General Fund reserve account established by the Legislature known as the Projected Surplus Temporary Holding Account, provided that the amount not subject to limitation may not exceed 10% of the amount of General Fund proceeds of taxes for the applicable fiscal year. Funds withdrawn, transferred, or appropriated from those reserve accounts, if they were not counted previously as appropriations subject to limitation of the State when deposited, would constitute appropriations subject to limitation of the State in the fiscal year in which the withdrawal, transfer, or appropriation occurs.

## Bill TextResolved by the Assembly, the Senate concurring, That the Legislature of the State of California at its 2025–26 Regular Session commencing on the second day of December 2024, two-thirds of the membership of each house concurring, hereby proposes to the people of the State of California that the Constitution of the State be amended as follows:

### First—

 (a) This measure shall be known, and may be cited, as the Save for California’s Future Act.

(b) The Legislature finds and declares all of the following:

(1) California families understand that responsible financial planning requires setting aside savings during good times to prepare for unexpected challenges and economic downturns. The State of California should follow the same commonsense principle.

(2) Californians expect their government to manage public finances responsibly, prudently, and with an eye toward future generations. Maintaining adequate reserves helps ensure that essential public services remain available when they are needed most.

(3) California’s economy is among the largest and most dynamic in the world, but it is also subject to economic cycles, fluctuations in revenue, natural disasters, public health emergencies, and other unforeseen events that can place significant strain on the state budget.

(4) When state revenues decline during economic downturns, insufficient reserves can force difficult choices that disrupt essential programs and services relied upon by California families, students, seniors, veterans, workers, and businesses.

(5) Building and maintaining strong budget reserves during periods of economic growth helps protect Californians from sudden reductions in essential services and reduces the need for drastic corrective actions during periods of fiscal stress.

(6) Sound financial planning requires looking beyond the next fiscal year and preparing for future challenges before they arise. Just like families save for emergencies and unexpected expenses, California should save during good years to protect schools, public safety, and essential services during tough times.

(7) Strong reserve policies promote fiscal stability, improve public confidence in state government, support long-term economic growth, and help preserve California’s ability to respond effectively to emergencies and economic downturns.

(8) Proposition 98 was enacted by the voters in 1988 to provide a minimum funding level for schools. Nothing in this act is intended to change the calculation or funding of the minimum guarantee under Section 8 of Article XVI.

(c) It is therefore the intent of the Legislature to strengthen the state’s commitment to responsible budgeting, long-term financial planning, and prudent savings by enhancing California’s budget reserves and ensuring that the state is better prepared for future economic challenges. Strengthening reserves is an investment in California’s future and in future generations.

# CA 

Prop 2

| Constitutional Amendment

## Increases State’s Rainy Day Fund

Increases the maximum balance of the state’s rainy day reserves from 10% to 20%, changes how deposits and withdrawals from the account are calculated and authorized, exempts deposits from state spending caps, and expands mandatory repayment of certain debts and unfunded liabilities.

[](https://www.facebook.com/sharer/sharer.php?u=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.spur.org%2Fvoter-guide%2F2026-11%2Fca-prop-2-rainy-day-fund&title=California%20Prop%202%20-%20Rainy%20Day%20Fund "Share on Facebook") [](https://twitter.com/intent/tweet?url=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.spur.org%2Fvoter-guide%2F2026-11%2Fca-prop-2-rainy-day-fund&text=California%20Prop%202%20-%20Rainy%20Day%20Fund "Share on Twitter") [](https://www.linkedin.com/sharing/share-offsite/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.spur.org%2Fvoter-guide%2F2026-11%2Fca-prop-2-rainy-day-fund "Share on LinkedIn") [](/cdn-cgi/l/email-protection# "Share via Email") 

### SPUR's Recommendation

Given the volatile nature of California’s tax revenue structure, adequate reserve requirements are necessary to avoid severe service reductions during economic downturns. The proposed measure would better manage this boom-and-bust cycle by requiring greater savings during good times to avoid deeper reductions during bad ones — when public safety-net services are most needed.

##### Vote YES

![](/themes/custom/spur5/images/voter-guide/yes-highlight.svg) 

## **What Prop. 2 Would Do**

Proposition 2 would modify California’s Budget Stabilization Account (the state’s rainy day fund) to

*   Increase the maximum reserve balance from 10% to 20% of the state’s annual general fund revenues.
*   Require additional revenue deposits to increase the reserve and repay certain state long-term debts during periods of extraordinary revenue growth.
*   Expand the definition of long-term debts eligible for repayment from the reserve and extend these requirements from 2030 to 2040.
*   Clarify the account’s interaction with state constitutional limits on appropriations (setting funds aside for a specific purpose).

## **The Backstory**

California’s tax system produces volatile revenues because it relies heavily on personal income taxes, particularly capital gains. Consequently, revenues rise when the economy and stock market are strong and can fall by billions during downturns, creating boom-and-bust budget cycles. The Legislative Analyst’s Office (LAO) notes that these swings are an inherent feature of California’s revenue structure and are likely to continue, making a strong reserve policy an important tool for maintaining stable public services over time.[1](#_ftn1)

In response, California voters approved Proposition 2 in 2014, establishing a constitutional rainy day reserve known as the Budget Stabilization Account. During strong revenue years, the state must put half of excess revenues into the reserve until the reserve totals 10% of annual General Fund revenues. The other half must be used to pay down specific long-term debts and liabilities through 2030. According to the LAO, Proposition 2 has substantially improved California’s fiscal resilience, allowing the state to build larger reserves that have helped cushion recent budget deficits.[2](#_ftn2) Nevertheless, the LAO concludes that the current reserve structure remains insufficient to offset the magnitude of California’s long-term revenue volatility, leaving the state vulnerable to significant budget reductions during prolonged downturns. While California’s reserves have grown, they remain relatively low: the state ranks fifth in the nation for revenue volatility but only twenty-eighth for reserve levels.[3](#_ftn3)

This election’s Prop. 2 seeks to strengthen California’s reserve framework by increasing both the size of required reserve deposits and the maximum amount the state may accumulate in the reserve. The measure would double the constitutional cap on the reserve from 10% to 20%, require larger deposits to the reserve during years of exceptionally strong capital gains tax revenue growth, broaden the defined debts that may be paid down with other required deposits, and extend these debt payment obligations from 2030 to 2040.

The LAO concludes that these changes would allow California to save substantially more during boom years and better prepare for future recessions, although it also notes that even larger reserves would ultimately provide greater long-term protection against the state’s unusually volatile revenue base. The LAO estimates that the current reserve equal to 10% of revenues would cover about 30% of future budget gaps, while the proposed 20% reserve would cover about half of future gaps.

Finally, Prop. 2 would make several constitutional and procedural changes related to the state appropriations limit established by the Gann Limit, which imposes requirements on how the state can spend General Fund revenues. Under current law, reserve deposits count toward the appropriations limit when made, even though the funds are merely set aside rather than spent. The measure would instead count withdrawals from these accounts (spending), rather than deposits (setting funds aside). This approach better aligns the appropriations limit with the state’s reserve policy by allowing the state to save excess revenues without triggering the spending limit, while ensuring those funds count against the limit when ultimately spent.

The California Legislature placed the measure on the ballot, and it requires a simple majority (50% plus one vote) for approval.

## **Equity Impacts**

Over time, the measure would improve services for vulnerable communities that disproportionately rely on state-administered and state-funded programs. By building reserves during better economic times to minimize state budget reductions during recessions and economic downturns, the state would be better able to meet demand for public safety-net services, which often increases during those periods.

## **Pros**

*   Prop. 2 would improve the state’s rainy day account requirements to better manage the boom-and-bust nature of the state’s volatile revenue structure, better matching spending and revenues over time.
*   By improving the stability of the state’s fiscal management, the measure would benefit California city and county governments that often face state budget reductions during economic downturns.
*   By extending mandatory requirements to pay down debts and long-term liabilities, the measure would reduce the state’s long-term costs.
*   The measure would rationalize the reserve’s interaction with state constitutional appropriation limit requirements.

## **Con**

*   The maximum required balance for the Budget Stabilization Account would cover only about 50% of revenue losses during a typical economic downturn.

{"type":"WebSearch","query":"California Projected Surplus Temporary Holding Account Government Code 16418.7 what is it Gann limit","content":"**The Projected Surplus Temporary Holding Account (established by California Government Code § 16418.7) is a temporary General Fund reserve created in 2024 as a pilot budgeting tool to set aside a portion of anticipated surplus revenues for up to one year, helping manage tax revenue volatility without immediately spending funds that might not fully materialize.**[[1]](https://california.public.law/codes/government_code_section_16418.7)

It was added by AB 179 (Stats. 2024, Ch. 997, effective September 30, 2024) as Article 7.6.3 of the Government Code. Key provisions include:

- It holds surplus General Fund moneys temporarily for use in future fiscal years as a “responsible budgeting technique.”
- Transfers into the account must be specified in the annual Budget Act.
- Funds (plus any interest/earnings) cannot stay longer than one year from deposit; they then return to the General Fund unless the next Budget Act appropriates them for other purposes.
- The State Controller may use the funds for cash-flow loans to the General Fund.
- It is a pilot program that sunsets December 31, 2030 (with legislative intent to potentially extend it based on experience).

State leaders have used it in practice—for example, the 2026-27 Budget Act transferred $6.4 billion into the account for allocation in 2027-28. It functions as a short-term holding mechanism alongside other reserves like the Budget Stabilization Account (BSA, or “rainy day fund”) and Special Fund for Economic Uncertainties (SFEU).[[2]](https://ebudget.ca.gov/2026-27/pdf/Enacted/BudgetSummary/Introduction.pdf)

### Connection to the Gann Limit
The **Gann Limit** (officially the State Appropriations Limit or SAL) is California’s constitutional spending cap, added by Proposition 4 (1979) as Article XIII B of the state Constitution. Placed on the ballot by the California Legislature this summer via Assembly Constitutional Amendment 20, Proposition 2 asks voters to approve changes to the state budget process. On its face, it doesn’t seem too bad and the title given to it for the ballot is seemingly innocuous, “Increases State’s Rainy Day Fund. Legislative Constitutional Amendment.”

As the title and summary suggest, passage of Prop. 2 would double the state budget reserve cap from 10% of General Fund revenues to 20% of General Fund revenues. The General Fund is the state’s main spending account.

Supporters build off the intuition voters may have about the virtues of saving and having a bigger “rainy day fund.” As the author statement in support of ACA 20 argues, “By strengthening California’s Rainy Day Fund, we can protect funding for schools and essential public services, better weather future economic downturns, and leave our children a stronger, more resilient California.”

That argument does key in on a recurring problem facing state government financing, which is its volatility given the state’s heavy reliance on income and capital gains taxes, which are prone to boom and bust cycles. Consistently, the state has succumbed to the temptations of spending more, creating new programs, funding more boondoggles like the California High-Speed Rail project. Then, when the money runs out, the state panics, abruptly slashes some spending and plays budget shell games like borrowing from other state funds to cover General Fund spending.

That gets to the core problem with Prop. 2. The state doesn’t actually have a revenue problem. After accounting for inflation, the state budget has grown 40% since Gov. Gavin Newsom took office. There’s plenty of money coming in. The problem is how the state handles that money, which is irresponsibly.

In 2014, California voters approved another Proposition 2 which built on the state’s reserve rules and required the state to set aside 1.5% of General Fund revenue. Half had to go into the Budget Stabilization Fund, and half toward paying down debt. That latter provision is set to expire in 2030.

Enter the 2026 Prop. 2, which would enable some of the worst behavior of the Legislature, including its practice of borrowing from other state funds, by expanding the types of debts that would count as lawful uses of that money and extending that authorization through 2040.

It’s easy to miss, but the LAO summary of Prop. 2 in the official voter guide mailed out to everyone actually mentions this: “Specifically, these payments could be used to make required payments to schools and community colleges, repay borrowing from other state funds, and repay certain loans from the federal government.” As columnist and editorial board member Susan Shelley [notes](/2026/09/26/proposition-2-isnt-about-saving-money-its-another-sacramento-shell-game/), “This effectively relieves the state’s General Fund of these IOU payment obligations, freeing up billions of dollars of General Fund revenue for more spending.”

Finally, as noted by Assemblymen David Tangipa and Carl DeMaio, along with Senator Steven Choi, “Prop. 2 creates loopholes and accounting gimmicks so politicians can eliminate any chance of you getting your tax rebate.” What they are referring to is the state constitutional spending cap known as the Gann Limit which, though weakened over the years, requires the state to give rebates to taxpayers under certain circumstances. Vote no on Prop. 2 and elect more prudent state lawmakers.

## Overview

### How would Proposition 2 change transfers and the cap for the state's Budget Stabilization Account?

*See also: [Measure desing](#Measure_design)*

As of 2026, the state transfers 1.5% of estimated general fund revenues into the BSA each year. The California Department of Finance separately calculates the share of general fund revenue derived from personal income taxes paid on capital gains, and the portion exceeding 8% of total general fund proceeds of taxes forms the basis for an additional deposit. Proposition 2 would maintain this treatment for capital gains revenue between 8% and 10%, and would count revenue above 10% at 150% of its value. The resulting total is reduced by the increase in the state's [Proposition 98](/California_Proposition_98,_Mandatory_Education_Spending_Initiative_\(1988\) "California Proposition 98, Mandatory Education Spending Initiative (1988)") education funding obligation. Half of what remains, along with half of the 1.5% transfer, is deposited into the BSA, and the other half goes to debt repayment. Proposition 2 would extend that 50-50 split through the 2039-2040 fiscal year and would add federal loans made to the state's Unemployment Fund to the obligations eligible for repayment.[\[1\]](#cite_note-text-1) 

Proposition 2 would also increase the maximum balance of the BSA from 10% to 20% of estimated general fund proceeds of taxes. Under existing law, which Proposition 2 would not change, general fund proceeds of taxes that would have been transferred to the account but exceed the cap may be spent only on infrastructure, including deferred maintenance. According to the California Budget & Policy Center, the BSA balance reached the cap in two fiscal years — 2022-2023 and 2023-2024 — before dropping below it as funds were withdrawn to address budget shortfalls.[\[1\]](#cite_note-text-1)[\[2\]](#cite_note-2) 

### How would Proposition 2 change how transfers are counted in relation to the state's spending limit (Gann Limit)?

*See also: [Measure desing](#Measure_design)*

The state's spending limit, also known as the Gann Limit — established by [Proposition 4 (1979)](/California_Proposition_4,_Government_Spending_%27Gann_Limit%27_Initiative_\(1979\) "California Proposition 4, Government Spending 'Gann Limit' Initiative (1979)") and named after its sponsor, Paul Gann — caps annual state and local government appropriations financed from tax revenue and certain fee revenue at the prior year's limit, adjusted for changes in the cost of living and population. Deposits into the BSA currently count against that limit as appropriations subject to limitation.[\[1\]](#cite_note-text-1) 

Beginning with the 2027-28 fiscal year, Proposition 2 would exclude deposits into the BSA from the limit. Funds later withdrawn from the account that were not counted when deposited would instead count against the limit in the fiscal year they are withdrawn or returned to the general fund. The measure would apply the same treatment to the Projected Surplus Temporary Holding Account, a general fund reserve account established in statute in 2024, except that no more than 10% of general fund proceeds of taxes could be excluded in any year.[\[1\]](#cite_note-text-1) 

### Who supports and opposes Proposition 2?

*See also: [Support](#Support) and [Opposition](#Opposition)*

Ballotpedia has not identified any committees registered to support or oppose Proposition 2. The amendment was placed on the ballot with unanimous support from voting Democrats, while 9% of voting Republicans supported it. Senate President pro Tempore [Monique Limón](/Monique_Lim%C3%B3n "Monique Limón") (D-21) said, "The Rainy Day Fund is critical to the annual California State Budget and helps mitigate cuts to state programs in difficult budget years. California has faced tough decisions, requiring legislators to dip into the fund to help fill the gaps — but there is more work to be done. Boosting the Rainy Day Fund will continue to provide a needed reserve for future years and protect programs that working families need."[\[3\]](#cite_note-Overview-3)[\[4\]](#cite_note-4) 

State Asm. [Joe Patterson](/Joe_Patterson "Joe Patterson") (R-5), who voted against placing the amendment on the ballot, said, "We don’t have a rainy day fund in California. All this does is create a bigger slush fund for money to be used the following years instead of returning the money to the taxpayer."[\[5\]](#cite_note-5)

Changes to Budget Stabilization Account deposits and cap

Proposition 2 would amend Sections 20 and 22 of [Article XVI](/Article_XVI,_California_Constitution "Article XVI, California Constitution") of the [California Constitution](/California_Constitution "California Constitution"), which govern the Budget Stabilization Account (BSA) and the Public School System Stabilization Account (PSSSA). Both sections were added by [Proposition 2](/California_Proposition_2,_Changes_to_State_Budget_Stabilization_Fund_Amendment_\(2014\) "California Proposition 2, Changes to State Budget Stabilization Fund Amendment (2014)") in 2014.

Currently, the state controller transfers a sum equal to 1.5% of estimated general fund revenues to the BSA each fiscal year. In addition, the California Department of Finance (DOF) calculates the portion of general fund proceeds of taxes derived from personal income taxes paid on net capital gains that exceeds 8% of total general fund proceeds of taxes, reduced by the resulting increase in the state's [Proposition 98](/California_Proposition_98,_Mandatory_Education_Spending_Initiative_\(1988\) "California Proposition 98, Mandatory Education Spending Initiative (1988)") education funding obligation. Through the 2029-30 fiscal year, 50% of both amounts is transferred to the BSA, and the other 50% is appropriated by the [California State Legislature](/California_State_Legislature "California State Legislature") for specified debts and liabilities. The balance of the account may not exceed 10% of estimated general fund proceeds of taxes.[\[1\]](#cite_note-text-1) 

Beginning with the 2027-2028 fiscal year, Proposition 2 would replace the single 8% threshold with a two-tier calculation. The DOF would instead report the sum of the following to the state legislature:[\[1\]](#cite_note-text-1) 

*   capital gains revenue in excess of 8%, but not in excess of 10%, of general fund proceeds of taxes; and
*   150% of capital gains revenue in excess of 10% of general fund proceeds of taxes.

This sum would not be deposited into the BSA directly. It serves as the basis for the deposit calculation, which subtracts the resulting Proposition 98 obligation, splits the remainder between the BSA and debt repayment through the 2039-40 fiscal year, and is capped by the account's maximum balance. 

Proposition 2 would extend the 50-50 split between BSA deposits and debt repayment through the 2039-40 fiscal year, rather than the 2029-30 fiscal year under existing law. It would also make the following changes to the obligations for which the debt repayment half may be appropriated:[\[1\]](#cite_note-text-1) 

*   add federal loans made to the state's Unemployment Fund;
*   remove the July 1, 2014, cutoff on unfunded Proposition 98 obligations, making all such obligations eligible;
*   add earlier-than-scheduled recognition of the costs of loans made to the Medical Providers Interim Payment Fund and of costs described in Section 41206.04 of the Education Code; and
*   provide that if the appropriation exceeds the total of the eligible obligations, the remainder would be transferred to the BSA, subject to the account's balance cap.

Proposition 2 would increase the maximum balance of the BSA from 10% to 20% of estimated general fund proceeds of taxes.[\[1\]](#cite_note-text-1) 

Proposition 2 would apply the two-tier calculation to the updated estimates that the DOF prepares for prior fiscal years, which are used to true up deposits against actual revenues. It would also reset the fiscal years on which these calculations are based, replacing references to the 2015-16 through 2017-18 fiscal years with the 2026-27 through 2028-29 fiscal years.

Gann Limit changes

The Gann Limit, established by [Proposition 4 (1979)](/California_Proposition_4,_Government_Spending_%27Gann_Limit%27_Initiative_\(1979\) "California Proposition 4, Government Spending 'Gann Limit' Initiative (1979)") and named after the sponsor of Proposition 4, Paul Gann, limits the total annual appropriations subject to limitation of the state to the prior year's limit, adjusted for changes in the cost of living and population. Deposits into the BSA currently count against that limit as appropriations subject to limitation.[\[1\]](#cite_note-text-1)

Beginning with the 2027-28 fiscal year, Proposition 2 would provide that transfers to the BSA do not constitute appropriations subject to limitation. Funds later withdrawn from the account, or returned to the general fund, that were not counted previously would constitute appropriations subject to limitation in the fiscal year in which the withdrawal or return occurred.[\[1\]](#cite_note-text-1) 

Proposition 2 would apply the same treatment to the Projected Surplus Temporary Holding Account, except that the amount excluded in any fiscal year could not exceed 10% of general fund proceeds of taxes for that year.[\[1\]](#cite_note-text-1)

Changes to budget emergency declarations

Proposition 2 would provide that the revised budget proposal that the director of finance submits to the state legislature in May would itself constitute the governor's proclamation of budget emergency if the revision proposes suspending or reducing transfers from the general fund to the BSA or the PSSSA, returning money from the BSA to the general fund, or appropriating money from the PSSSA. A separate proclamation from the governor would not be required, but the following constitutional conditions for a budget emergency would still also apply:[\[1\]](#cite_note-text-1)

*   a disaster is declared by the governor or
*   the governor determines that general fund expenditures — measured against the highest of the last three enacted budgets' expenditure estimates adjusted for inflation and population growth — exceed the state's resources for the current or next fiscal year.

## Prediction markets

*See also: [Prediction markets](/Prediction_markets "Prediction markets")*

A prediction market is a platform where users buy and sell contracts tied to the outcome of future events. The price of a contract reflects the market's estimated probability of that outcome — a contract priced at 55 cents suggests the market estimates a 55 percent chance the event occurs. Volume reflects how actively a market is being traded.[\[11\]](#cite_note-11) Unlike polls, which survey a sample of voters, prediction markets aggregate the financial stakes of individual bettors. A market with higher trading volume is generally considered more reliable than one with low volume, though prices can be influenced by large individual traders.

## Background

### Budget Stabilization Account

The Budget Stabilization Account (BSA) was created with the approval of [Proposition 58](/California_Proposition_58,_Balanced_Budget_Amendment_\(March_2004\) "California Proposition 58, Balanced Budget Amendment (March 2004)") in 2004. It required 3% of general fund revenue to be deposited into the account annually regardless of economic performance. Proposition 58 also required the [California State Legislature](/California_State_Legislature "California State Legislature") to pass a balanced budget. After the first deposit in 2007, the state suspended transfers due to the Great Recession through fiscal year 2013-2014.[\[12\]](#cite_note-12)[\[13\]](#cite_note-13) 

In 2014, California voters approved [Proposition 2](/California_Proposition_2,_Changes_to_State_Budget_Stabilization_Fund_Amendment_\(2014\) "California Proposition 2, Changes to State Budget Stabilization Fund Amendment (2014)"), requiring 1.5% of general fund revenues and an amount equal to revenues derived from capital gains-related taxes in situations when such tax revenues are in excess of 8% of general fund revenues to be deposited into the BSA. 

The first withdrawal from the fund was made during the 2020-2021 fiscal year due to the economic impacts of the COVID-19 pandemic.[\[14\]](#cite_note-14) 

In June 2024, Gov. [Gavin Newsom](/Gavin_Newsom "Gavin Newsom") (D) declared a budget emergency according to [Section 22 of Article XVI](/Article_XVI,_California_Constitution#Section_22 "Article XVI, California Constitution") of the state constitution after determining estimated resources would be inadequate to fund general fund expenditures for the current or following fiscal year. The declaration authorized the state legislature to suspend the annual transfer to the BSA. The state withdrew $12.2 billion from the BSA between 2024 and 2026.[\[15\]](#cite_note-15)[\[16\]](#cite_note-16)
